chunks: Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ali ibn al-Hakam from al-'Ala' from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'The woman inherits the 'Tub' (the main male ancestor/stock), and she does not inherit anything from the 'Ribaa' (the other males). I said: 'How does she inherit from the 'Far' (offspring/descendants) and not inherit anything from the 'Ribaa'? He said to me: 'She has no kinship with them by which she inherits, and she is an outsider to them; therefore she inherits from the 'Far' and does not inherit from the 'Asl' (the main stock), and no one enters their [lineage] through her.'

key_terms.الرِّبَاع: The 'Ribaa', referring to the collateral males or other branches of the family
key_terms.الطُّوب: The 'Tub' or main ancestral stock/stock of the family
key_terms.الْأَصْل: The 'Asl', referring to the main root or primary lineage
key_terms.الْفَرْع: The 'Far', referring to offspring or descendants
key_terms.دَخِيل: An outsider or affiliate who joins a group but is not of the core lineage

ai.seo_question: How does a woman inherit from her husband's family according to the distinction between 'Far' and 'Ribaa'?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the principle of 'inheritance by connection' (*nasab al-sabab*) versus 'inheritance by blood' (*nasab al-asl*), establishing that a wife inherits from her husband's descendants because she is linked to them, yet her own lineage does not merge with his for the purpose of her relatives inheriting from his main stock. It highlights the Shia juristic distinction where the female spouse is an affiliate (*dakhil*) to the husband's patrilineal line, inheriting from the 'branch' (descendants) but not contributing to the 'root' (ancestors/collaterals) in the same manner. This reflects the broader Islamic legal concept that marriage creates a bond of inheritance without altering the fundamental genealogical lineage (*nasab*) of the parties involved.
